name: Wei Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you would say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm at the depot by half seven, scan my bags into the driver app and load the electric van. I do the hill route, Ridge Road and the estates above it, about 130 drops a day. Most drivers hate it because of the steps, which is exactly why it pays better. Fridays and Saturdays I do takeaway on two food apps in my own hatchback for a few extra hours.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being on my own with the radio and nobody standing over me. I know which dogs bite and which old man wants a chat. What wears me out is the app changing the drop order at ten past eight and my knees on those steps. Hana (my girlfriend) says I come home walking like her granddad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what everyone at the depot already says, which is that the app was meant to be smart years ago and it still sends me down a dead end twice a week. Online I'd probably just post a meme about it. Nobody's going to argue about AI over the lunch van if nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means not much. The app already tells me which door to knock on. If AI only gets a bit better at that, I'm still the one carrying the dog food up the hill. My pay stays where it is and I keep saving for the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the hill route, because nobody else wants it and that's my bargaining card on pay. I'd keep putting about 600 a month into the deposit pot and aim to buy a two-bed with Hana in about two years. Maybe I'd let a chatbot sort my tax forms again, like I did last spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels fine, normal. Bit boring, maybe. The only thing that nags me is my knees, and that's got nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your knees. How long do you think your body lasts on the hill route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, maybe less on the hill. Tomasz (an older driver at the depot) is 54 and he's on the flat routes now because his back went. I don't want to be him at 54, so I'd want to be doing something else by my late thirties anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight in that world, what would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First would be the Friday night food shifts, because they're extra and they wreck my weekends. Hana would be happy about that. The van work stays, because it's the real money.

say: Nothing changes if AI is **mostly hype**; the app still sends me down **dead ends**.
I'd joke about it online rather than **argue** about it at the depot.
think: My **pay** and the flat plan stay on track if AI barely improves.
The real limit is my **knees**, not technology; ten years on the hill at most.
do: Keep the **hill route** because it pays more and nobody else wants it.
Save about **600 a month** towards a two-bed flat with Hana within two years.
Use a chatbot for **tax forms** again, as he did last spring.
feel: He feels **settled** and a bit bored by this picture.
His only nag is his **body**, which has nothing to do with AI.
S0.quote: The app already tells me which door to knock on. If AI only gets a bit better at that, I'm still the one carrying the dog food up the hill.
fieldNote: He treats the hill route's steps as his **bargaining card** on pay, a smart read of a tough route.
His real timeline is set by his **body**, with an older colleague as the warning.
Strong savings and plenty of local driving work make this picture feel **secure** to him.

steps.text: Keep the hill route and its higher pay at the depot
Put about 600 a month into the flat deposit pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people who should worry this time, not us. At the depot I'd say robots can't climb steps yet, so we're fine for now. Online I'd keep it short, because people get nasty about this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the depot gets leaner. The planners and the people who answer complaints get replaced by software, and then the software pushes us harder with tighter slots. Robots can't climb the steps on Ridge Road with a 20-kilo parcel yet. I'd use the slow years to get a trade, not to sit and hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by asking my cousin Lukas, who's an electrician, what an apprenticeship really pays and how long it takes. If it looked solid after a few months, I'd sign up for the evening course at the college, the one that's two nights a week. I'd keep the van in the day and drop the Friday food shifts to make room. I'd also start using the route tools properly instead of fighting them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, I suppose. Not scared, because I've got the savings and there's driving work everywhere. It's more like hearing a noise in the van that you can't place yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The one who'd get it first is the woman who does our complaints line, Rosa (the depot's customer service lead). She's great with angry customers, but that's exactly the kind of thing the card says AI takes. Tomasz worries me too, because he hates the app as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you're fine, but you're also signing up for a course. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really a contradiction. I'm calm about this year and next year. I'm thinking about the year I'm 33, and that's when I want the trade done.

say: This round hits the **office staff** first, not drivers who climb steps.
I'd keep comments **short online** because the topic gets nasty fast.
think: Software will replace **planners** and complaints staff, then push drivers with **tighter slots**.
The slow arrival of robots is **time** to learn a **trade**, not time to relax.
do: Ask his cousin Lukas what an **electrician apprenticeship** pays and how long it takes.
Sign up for the **evening course** at the college, two nights a week.
Drop the **Friday food shifts** to make room and learn the route tools properly.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, like an unexplained noise in the van, but not scared.
His savings and plentiful driving jobs keep him from **real fear**.
S1.quote: Robots can't climb the steps on Ridge Road with a 20-kilo parcel yet. I'd use the slow years to get a trade, not to sit and hope.
fieldNote: He reads the card through the **depot's office**, and expects the pressure to come back down onto drivers.
He thinks in **ages**, not years: the target is a trade by 33.
He worries for **colleagues** more readily than for himself.

steps.text: Ask cousin Lukas about electrician apprenticeship pay and length
Enrol in the college's two-night evening electrics course
Learn the depot's new route tools instead of fighting them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the bosses will try it on us first and see what sticks. Online I'd probably say governments should have seen it coming, which they should. I'd sound more relaxed than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028 means the depot office is gone and the app runs everything, every minute of my day. Then robots by 2031. Five years sounds like plenty when you're 27. Then I count it in Christmases, and it's five peak seasons left before a robot takes my van. That's not much at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrics course straight away, not wait to see if it's proven, because there's no time for that. I'd keep the van full time, because I'd need every bit of pay while I train. I'd talk to Hana about holding off on the flat for a year so the savings cover me if I end up on apprentice wages. I'd also take every overtime shift at peak season to top up the pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, if I'm honest. I like having a plan and a bit of time to check it works. This picture takes away the checking bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hana about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Hana the flat waits a year, and that I'd rather rent for longer than buy and then find I can't pay the mortgage on apprentice money. She'd be fine with it, I think; her job at the dental clinic isn't going anywhere fast. It'd be a long talk, but not a fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does it change for you that the robots come three years after the thinking AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots coming three years after the AI matters a lot to me. My job is nearly all hands-on, the lifting, the steps, the driving. So the AI part only changes the app and the office, and the robot part is the one that actually ends my job. Those three years are my training window.

say: I'd say the bosses will **test it on drivers** first and see what sticks.
Online I'd blame **governments** for not seeing it coming.
think: By 2028 the **app runs everything** and the depot office is gone.
Robots by 2031 leave him only **five peak seasons** before losing the van.
do: Start the **electrics course** immediately rather than waiting for proof.
Keep driving **full time** and take every peak-season overtime shift.
Put the **flat purchase** on hold for a year to protect the savings.
feel: He feels **anxious**, because this picture removes the time to check his plan.
He sounds calmer in public than he **really feels**.
S2.quote: Five years sounds like plenty when you're 27. Then I count it in Christmases, and it's five peak seasons left before a robot takes my van.
fieldNote: He is a **steady** type forced to move early; he dislikes acting without proof.
The three-year **robot lag** is the core of his plan: it is his training window.
Strong **savings** and his partner's stable job give him room to take apprentice wages.

steps.text: Start the college electrics course straight away this autumn
Take every peak-season overtime shift to top up savings
Hold off buying the two-bed flat with Hana for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them, and I'd say it to the younger lads at the depot too. Online I'd say the same, maybe share something about free courses if there were any. It's the sort of thing people ignore until it's late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years to the AI and eight to the robots, I honestly think I can land on my feet. With robots in 2034 I'd have time to finish an electrician's apprenticeship and still be under 35 when the vans go driverless. The danger is that everyone else has the same idea and the trades fill up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait about six months to see if the first changes at the depot match the picture, then start the course next autumn. I'd keep the van until I'm qualified, around 2030, and then switch to electrics with Lukas or a firm he knows. Hana and I would buy the flat on schedule, because by then I'd know my income path. I'd keep about eight months of costs in the bank the whole way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a manageable sort. I'd still lose the job I've got, I know that. It's just that I'd have time to walk out of it instead of being pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that every driver in town wants to be an electrician at the same time. Then I'm 31 and competing with 300 people for the same jobs. That's why I wouldn't wait the whole five years to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would electricians not be hit by the robots too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Building sites and rewiring jobs need hands, but the robots would come for those too, later. I've thought about that. I think an electrician who can fix the robots and the chargers lasts longer than a driver does.

say: I'd tell the **younger drivers** to use the few years they've got.
I'd share **free course** links online if any existed.
think: Robots by **2034** leave time to qualify as an electrician before 35.
The risk is a **flood** of drivers chasing the same trades.
do: Watch the depot for **six months**, then start the electrics course next autumn.
Keep driving until **qualified** around 2030, then switch to electrics.
Buy the **flat on schedule** while keeping eight months of costs saved.
feel: He feels **anxious** but in control, because he can leave rather than be pushed.
He expects to lose the **driving job** either way.
S3.quote: With robots in 2034 I'd have time to finish an electrician's apprenticeship and still be under 35 when the vans go driverless.
fieldNote: Five years suits his **steady** style: he wants six months of proof before acting.
He has thought ahead to **competition** for trade places, which few drivers mention.
He bets that **fixing robots and chargers** outlasts driving them.

steps.text: Watch depot changes for six months before enrolling
Start the electrician apprenticeship course next autumn
Switch to electrics work through Lukas once qualified around 2030
Keep eight months of living costs in the bank throughout

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and most predictions are wrong anyway. At the depot I'd say keep your head and get a second skill. Online I'd probably not say anything, because it would feel too far off to argue about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade is long enough that I'd be stupid to panic and stupid to do nothing. I'd be 37 when the robots come, which is when I wanted out of the hill route anyway. So in a way the timing almost suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat with Hana in two years as planned. I'd do the electrics course at a slower pace, one night a week, from about 2028. I'd keep the van and the hill pay until about 2033, then move over. Maybe I'd also try one of those AI tutors to help with the maths side, which is my weak bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly okay. It's far enough away to plan for and close enough to take seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What in your life would the extra time be for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kids, maybe. Hana and I have talked about having kids around 30. With ten years I'd want the trade sorted before then, so the baby isn't arriving during apprentice wages. So the course would probably start earlier than I'd normally like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it took longer than you hoped to switch, what would you cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to keep the house and the savings for the kids. The car would go first, I think; I'd sell the hatchback and just use the van and the bus. I've done that before for a few months.

say: Ten years is long, and **predictions** are often wrong.
At the depot I'd say get a **second skill** and keep calm.
think: Robots arriving when he is **37** fits his plan to leave the hill route anyway.
Ten years makes both panic and **doing nothing** foolish.
do: Buy the **flat with Hana** in two years as planned.
Start a **one-night-a-week** electrics course around 2028 using an AI tutor for maths.
Keep the van and **hill pay** until about 2033, then move over.
feel: He feels **mostly okay**, with a small edge of unease.
The timing feels **far enough** to plan and close enough to matter.
S4.quote: A decade is long enough that I'd be stupid to panic and stupid to do nothing.
fieldNote: The ten-year picture lines up with his **own exit plan** from the physical route.
Hoped-for **children around 30** push his retraining earlier than it would otherwise be.
He would sell his **hatchback** first if money got tight.

steps.text: Buy a two-bed flat with Hana in two years
Take a one-night-a-week electrics course from 2028
Use an AI tutor for the maths part of the course
Keep the hill route van job until about 2033

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. It's not the AI part, it's the robots three years later and only five peak seasons to sort myself out. I'm not scared of the robot. I'm scared of being 34 with a van licence and nothing else on my CV. What would help is a proper paid apprenticeship for drivers, where you can earn while you train instead of dropping to half pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who owns the robots. If the depot owns them, the money goes up, not to us. I'm not political, but that bit matters.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of the robot. I'm scared of being 34 with a van licence and nothing else on my CV.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old** parcel driver on the hill route that pays more, plus weekend food delivery shifts.
He lives with his girlfriend **Hana** and saves about 600 a month for a flat deposit.
He is **steady**: he likes proof before change, and plans in terms of his age and his knees.
He moves from calm in AI Plateau to **anxious** in the fast AGI picture, where robots end his driving.
His answer every time is an **electrician apprenticeship**, timed to the three-year robot lag.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because robots by 2031 leave him only **five peak seasons** to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** for drivers, so he can earn while training instead of halving his pay.
Clarity on **who owns the robots**, since he expects the money to go upwards.
